Our advice to founders who just closed: pick the one metric your next investor will ask about, and organise the next 6-9 months around moving it.

Capacity is arriving in Uzbekistan. Access is the next bottleneck.

Euronews reports that data-centre investment commitments in the country now exceed $6bn. Saudi-based DataVolt is building a 12-megawatt facility in Tashkent, due to be operational by the end of 2026, with a plan to reach 300 megawatts across regions. The government's Nvidia cluster, launched this summer, hit 90% utilisation in its first month.

The same report notes the catch: computing power remains expensive for many local startups, and some still rely on international cloud providers. Oxford Insights counts 180 AI-using Uzbek startups exporting to 80 countries.

Our view at AI Station: demand is already there, so the question is price and access, not hardware. For founders, that means designing products that are efficient on compute from day one: smaller models, caching, honest unit economics per request. For investors, it is a reason to ask how a team's inference cost scales before asking about its roadmap.

Tilmoch started as a second-year course project at Inha University in Tashkent. Muhammadsaid Mamasaidov wanted autocorrect for Uzbek, a language with two alphabets and 150-200 affixes that reshape every word. The first web version had no users.

There was no large Uzbek corpus, so the team bought rare books, scanned them and built a corpus of about 35,000 texts. That data became a translator built for Turkic languages, released in September 2024.

From the founder's interview with Digital Business and Astana Hub: 200,000 monthly users in Uzbekistan, MRR of $22-23K, and a $150K round in 2025 from AloqaVentures, IT Park Ventures and Yoshlar Ventures at a $1.5M valuation.

Our view at AIS Studio: founders here often dismiss local-language problems as too small. They are exactly where global LLMs are weakest, and data you collect by hand is hard for anyone to copy.

AI will not replace your team. It will replace parts of their week.

In May 2025 the ILO and Poland's NASK published a refined global index: 25% of global employment sits in occupations potentially exposed to generative AI. Their conclusion is clear: transformation, not replacement, is the most likely outcome. Clerical work is the most exposed.

What that looks like in a 20-person company in Tashkent:
- Sales: call summaries and the first draft of a commercial offer
- Finance: sorting invoices and flagging mismatches, with a person signing off
- HR: first-pass CV screening against a clear checklist
- Management: turning a 30-page report into two pages

None of these removes a role. They remove the hours people spend on copy-paste, so the same team can serve more clients.

The first step we recommend to companies is not a tool. It is a list: every team writes down three tasks it repeats every week. That list shows where AI pays off and where it does not.

Which repetitive task would you hand over first?

Part 3 of our AI glossary for founders: the 10 terms that show up as soon as you build a real product.

RAG. The model retrieves the relevant parts of your own documents before it answers.
Embedding. Text turned into numbers by meaning, so search works on meaning and not on exact keywords.
Vector database. Stores embeddings and finds the closest ones fast.
Context window. How much text the model can take into account at once.
AI agent. A system that plans steps and calls tools to finish a task.
Inference. The moment a trained model produces an answer. Your per-request cost lives here.
Multimodal. One model that handles text, images and audio.
Open-weight model. Published weights you can run on your own servers.
Guardrails. Rules that limit what the model says and does.
Evals. A fixed set of your real questions that you run the model against before every release.

Our view at AI Station: write evals before you build the agent. Without them, "the model works" is a guess.

Rereading notes feels like studying. Testing yourself is what shows the gaps.

Our AI Tool of the Week is Gemini Notebook, the tool Google renamed from NotebookLM in July. It works with the sources you add, which makes it good at one specific job: turning lecture notes or internal documents into quizzes and flashcards.

2. In the Studio panel, choose Quizzes or Flashcards.
3. Use the pencil icon to set difficulty (easy, medium or hard), the number of questions and a custom prompt.

The limitation is real. A quiz is only as good as the notes behind it: gaps and errors in the source come straight through. Check doubtful answers against the original material.

captions.linkedin:
If your deck says "AI-powered", an investor learns nothing.

At TechCrunch Disrupt 2025, Medha Agarwal of Defy made a sharp observation: the more a founder talks about AI in a pitch, the less AI the company likely uses. In the strongest companies, AI is built in, but it is not the core of the pitch.

What she wants to see instead: how the technology enables the product, a clear go-to-market plan, why the business will run more efficiently than incumbents, and an honest competitor slide.

A simple rewrite test we suggest to founders:
Before: "AI-powered CRM platform."
After: "Drafts the next step after every sales call, so a manager's reporting time drops from [X] to [Y] minutes."

The formula is what it does + for whom + which number moved. If you do not have the number yet, that is your next experiment, not a design problem for the slide.

Founders: which line in your deck would fail this test?

An AI summary of a 40-page tender is only useful if you can trust the numbers in it.

Anthropic's guidance on reducing hallucinations gives a simple rule for long documents: ask the model to extract word-for-word quotes first, then do the task using only those quotes. It also recommends explicitly allowing the model to say it does not know.

A prompt we suggest to procurement and sales teams:
"Extract verbatim quotes on contract value, payment terms, deadlines, penalties and required documents. Then write a one-page summary based only on those quotes. If something is not in the document, write 'Not in the document'."

Before the summary leaves your desk, check every number and date against the original, and read the penalty clause yourself. Anthropic's own note is blunt: these techniques reduce hallucinations but do not eliminate them, so critical information still needs validation.

Used this way, AI changes the job from reading 40 pages to checking a handful of quotes.

Managers: which document in your team would you test this on first?

At pre-seed, the first investor meeting is mostly a test of speed and clarity.

Michael Seibel of Y Combinator put it plainly in his guide to pitching: he is "much more interested in progress than genius ideas." What he tries to understand is how fast a team produces work.

Seibel's guide and Sequoia's pitch outline point to four things that carry the first meeting:

1. Two sentences on what the company does. Seibel's "Email Test": send them to a smart friend and see if they get it. Sequoia asks for one declarative sentence.
2. The team. How many founders, whether there is a technical co-founder, whether everyone is full time, how equity is split.
3. Progress. What you shipped in recent weeks and who used it.
4. Why now. Sequoia gives it a section of its own.

At AIS Ventures our early cheques are $25K-$100K, and at that size the deck matters less than these answers. Write all four on one page before you open the slides.

Part 4 of our AI glossary for founders: six terms that decide what your AI feature costs and how often it is wrong.

Token. The unit a language model reads and writes. API prices are quoted per million tokens. On Anthropic's pricing page, Claude Sonnet 5.5 costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, so long answers cost more than long questions.
Few-shot prompting. Putting a few worked examples inside the prompt.
Temperature. A setting that controls how random the output is.
Fine-tuning. A second, task-specific training pass on a pre-trained model.
Distillation. Training a smaller, faster model to imitate a larger one.
Hallucination. Plausible-sounding output that is factually wrong.

Definitions follow Google's Machine Learning Glossary.

Our view at AI Station: try few-shot prompts before you pay for fine-tuning. Adding good examples takes an afternoon. Fine-tuning needs a labelled dataset and a training run. The cheap test tells you whether the problem is the model or your instructions.
